# Technical Description: Soft Polyurethane Foam Molded Article

### 1. General Composition and Overview
The present invention relates to a soft polyurethane foam molded article manufactured by foam-molding a designated stock solution. The molded article is designed with a defined structural orientation anchored by a specific mounting surface, which serves as the primary contact or attachment interface. 

Structurally, the body of the molded article is not homogeneous; rather, it comprises a plurality of distinct layered parts. These layers are stacked sequentially in a vertical direction that extends perpendicularly relative to the plane of the mounting surface (i.e., along the axis running from the mounting surface toward the opposing back surface).

### 2. Intra-Layer Cellular Structure
Within the internal microstructure of each individual layered part, the geometry of the foaming cells follows a precise gradient. The shape of these cells is defined by a cell size ratio, determined by dividing a cell's lateral dimension by its vertical dimension. 

Within any given layered part, this cell size ratio increases progressively as the cells are positioned closer to the mounting surface. Consequently, as one moves toward the mounting surface within a single layer, the cells become increasingly flattened or elongated in the horizontal plane relative to their vertical height.

### 3. Inter-Layer Boundary Characteristics
In addition to the internal gradient within each layer, the molded article features a specific structural transition at the interfaces (boundaries) between adjacent vertical layers. 

At the boundary separating two adjacent layers:
* The cell size ratio in the layer positioned closer to the **mounting surface** is **lower** (more vertically proportioned or spherical).
* The cell size ratio in the adjacent layer positioned further toward the **back surface** is **higher** (more laterally elongated).

This dynamic creates a distinct structural step-change at every layer boundary, interrupting the intra-layer gradient and resetting the cell aspect ratio across the overall cross-section of the article.

### 4. Summary of Functional Microstructure
By combining a continuous intra-layer gradient (where cells flatten toward the mounting surface) with a discontinuous inter-layer transition at the boundaries (where the cell ratio drops across the boundary toward the mounting surface), the foam article achieves a highly engineered density and dynamic response profile. This customized cellular orientation provides optimized mechanical properties, such as tailored cushioning, energy absorption, and durability across the depth of the polyurethane foam.

# Development of Advanced Soft Polyurethane Foam Articles with Tailored Cellular Anisotropy

## 1. Introduction and Overview
Flexible and soft polyurethane (PU) foams are critical materials in modern ergonomic design, automotive seating, bedding, and specialized cushioning applications. Traditionally, achieving a balance between initial soft tactile feedback and deep-layer structural support required assembling distinct foam slabs with differing chemical formulations or densities. 

This text outlines a single-mold manufacturing approach that achieves localized, gradient-controlled mechanical performance within a unified soft polyurethane foam molded article. By precisely manipulating the cell morphology—specifically the lateral-to-vertical aspect ratio of individual foam cells across vertically stacked layers—a continuous yet structural gradient is formed. This architecture optimizes weight distribution, enhances dynamic energy absorption, and improves overall durability.

---

## 2. Chemical Composition and Stock Solution Processing
The underlying material matrix consists of a tailored polyurethane foaming stock solution. This formulation typically comprises:
* **Polyols:** A blend of high-molecular-weight polyether or polyester polyols designed for flexibility and elasticity.
* **Isocyanates:** Diisocyanates (such as MDI or TDI variants) calibrated to react with the polyol blend.
* **Blowing Agents:** Water and/or auxiliary blowing agents that generate carbon dioxide gas, driving the expansion of the polymer matrix.
* **Catalysts and Surfactants:** Organometallic and amine catalysts to balance the gelling and blowing reactions, alongside silicone surfactants that stabilize cell walls during expansion to control cell size and open-cell content.

During the molding process, the reaction kinetics and physical environment within the mold cavity are regulated to influence how gas bubbles nucleate, grow, elongate, and set.

---

## 3. Layered Architecture and Cell Geometry Dynamics

### 3.1 Definition of Cell Aspect Ratio
The cellular structure of the foam is characterized by an anisotropic cell ratio ($R$), defined as:

$$R = \frac{\text{Cell Size in the Lateral (Horizontal) Dimension}}{\text{Cell Size in the Vertical Dimension}}$$

* **Low Ratio ($R < 1$):** Cells are vertically elongated (prolate), resembling vertical columns. This configuration offers higher initial compressive strength and resistance to vertical buckling.
* **High Ratio ($R > 1$):** Cells are laterally flattened (oblate), oriented horizontally. This configuration yields a softer vertical compliance and higher lateral distribution of applied force.

```
       [ Back Surface Layer ]     --> Higher Ratio (R > 1) 
                                      (Laterally flattened, soft feel)
   =============================  <-- Layer Interface (R_lower < R_upper)
      [ Intermediate Layer ]
   =============================  <-- Layer Interface (R_lower < R_upper)
     [ Mounting Surface Layer ]   --> Lower Ratio (R < 1) 
                                      (Vertically elongated, high support)
```

### 3.2 Vertical Layer Stacking and Boundary Characteristics
The molded article is composed of a series of vertically stacked, integrated foam layers extending upward from a lower **mounting surface** (the side designed to attach to a frame or support plate) to an upper **back-surface layer** (or functional surface layer).

Rather than displaying a uniform cell geometry throughout, the foam exhibits controlled variation across adjacent layers:
1. **Gradient Behavior:** The cell size ratio ($R$) transitions systematically relative to proximity to the mounting surface.
2. **Interfacial Boundary Conditions:** At the boundary interface between any two adjacent layers, the cell size ratio in the lower layer (closer to the mounting surface) is strictly lower than the cell size ratio in the immediately adjacent upper layer (closer to the back surface).

$$\text{Ratio}_{\text{Mounting Side Interface}} < \text{Ratio}_{\text{Back-Surface Side Interface}}$$

This specific morphological step-change ensures that as load penetrates deeper into the foam toward the mounting surface, the structure transitions from a soft, compliant network into a stiffer, column-supported structure capable of resisting bottoming-out.

---

## 4. Manufacturing Control Principles
Achieving this differentiated cellular structure within a single molded component relies on controlling the thermal and physical variables during the foaming phase:

* **Differential Temperature Profiles:** Mold surfaces near the mounting area are maintained at specific thermal thresholds to influence foam skin formation and gas expansion rates, encouraging vertical cell stretching near the base.
* **Sequential In-Situ Pouring / Differential Expansion:** The foaming stock solution is introduced in controlled stages or with variable nucleation pressures, allowing lower layers to set under slight internal hydrostatic pressure while upper layers expand more freely in the lateral direction.
* **Dynamic Mold Manipulation:** Variable pressure release mechanisms or localized mechanical vibrations are applied during the gel-transition phase to orient cell windows prior to full polymer network crosslinking.

---

## 5. Mechanical Performance and Practical Advantages

By engineered variation of the lateral-to-vertical cell ratios across structural boundaries, the resulting polyurethane article demonstrates several performance advantages over isotropic foams:

1. **Progressive Load Deflection:** The upper layers (higher $R$) yield easily to localized light loads, delivering high surface comfort. As the load increases, deeper layers (lower $R$) engage, providing strong vertical column support.
2. **Enhanced Shear Energy Dissipation:** The distinct structural transitions at layer boundaries disrupt unified stress propagation paths, effectively dissipating lateral shear forces and improving dynamic vibration damping.
3. **Weight-to-Performance Optimization:** High structural integrity and load-bearing capacity are achieved without increasing overall chemical density, yielding lightweight components with enhanced fatigue resistance.

---

## 6. Applications
This gradient-cell foam technology is well-suited for high-performance applications where comfort, ergonomic support, and space constraints intersect:
* **Automotive and Transportation Seating:** Provides smooth initial contact feel combined with firm support during long transport and dynamic vehicle maneuvers.
* **Ergonomic Furniture and Bedding:** Adapts to body contours while maintaining proper spinal alignment through targeted zonal support.
* **Impact and Vibration Isolation Components:** Serves as high-durability dampening pads in industrial, aerospace, and medical equipment applications.

**The Architecture of "The"**

It is comprised of just three simple letters, yet it holds an absolute monopoly over the English language. It is the first word we learn to read, the most frequently typed sequence on our keyboards, and the quiet foundation upon which almost every sentence rests. Yet, because of its overwhelming ubiquity, we rarely stop to consider the extraordinary power of the word **"the."**

Linguistically, "the" is known as the definite article. On the surface, its job is mundane: it points at nouns. But philosophically, "the" is a tool of profound transformation. It possesses the unique ability to collapse an infinity of possibilities down to a single, specific reality. 

Consider the vast distance between "a" and "the." 

If someone says, "I am looking for *a* house," they are embarking on an open-ended search through a world of endless options. But when they say, "I am looking for *the* house," the tone instantly shifts. The search is narrowed; a destination has been decided. "A moment" is just a random slice of ticking time, easily forgotten. "*The* moment" is a turning point in history, a memory etched in stone. To live "a life" is merely biological, but to live "*the* life" implies purpose, fulfillment, and distinction.

In this way, "the" acts as a spotlight. It rescues objects, people, and concepts from the sea of generalities and grants them singularity. It tells the listener that the speaker is not talking about just anything—they are talking about *this* specific thing, a shared point of reference between two minds. When you ask a friend, "Did you see *the* moon tonight?" the word "the" instantly bridges the gap between you, pointing both of your eyes toward the same celestial body in a vast sky.

Furthermore, "the" carries the weight of authority and supremacy. To be called "a expert" sounds modest, but to be acknowledged as "*the* expert" confers unmatched prestige. Titles like *The King*, *The Matrix*, or *The Beatles* utilize the word to claim a singular identity, declaring that no substitute will suffice.

Without this tiny three-letter titan, our language would crumble into disjointed, telegram-style fragments. It is the invisible glue of thought, the anchor of context, and the subtle painter of detail. "The" teaches us that true meaning often resides not in the grandest, most complex vocabulary, but in the smallest words that choose where we direct our attention.

***

# SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

The present disclosure relates generally to cellular polymeric structures and, more particularly, to a foam-molded article having adjacent vertical layers exhibiting differing cell geometries at their interfacial boundary to provide enhanced mechanical, structural, or energy-absorptive performance.

### Technical Problem
Conventional foam-molded articles often exhibit uniform cellular structures throughout their bulk or continuous gradients that fail to optimize mechanical requirements across different functional zones. In multi-layer or vertically stacked foam structures, poor interfacial bonding, abrupt stress concentration, or mismatched deformation behaviors under load frequently lead to delamination, premature shear failure, or suboptimal energy absorption. There is a need for a foam-molded structure that addresses these limitations through controlled local cell morphology at layer boundaries.

### Solution and Technical Features
To address the aforementioned challenges, the present disclosure provides a foam-molded article engineered with distinct, localized cell geometries across adjacent vertical layers, particularly at or near their shared boundary.

In one aspect of the present disclosure, a foam-molded article comprises:
*   a first vertical layer comprising a first cellular foam structure; and
*   a second vertical layer comprising a second cellular foam structure, the second vertical layer disposed adjacent to the first vertical layer along a vertical axis to define a boundary region therebetween;
*   wherein the first cellular foam structure exhibits a first cell aspect ratio ($C_1$) at the boundary region, and the second cellular foam structure exhibits a second cell aspect ratio ($A_2$) at the boundary region, such that $C_1$ is mathematically different from $A_2$ ($C_1 \neq A_2$).

For the purposes of this disclosure, the cell aspect ratio refers to the ratio of a cell's major dimension to its minor dimension (e.g., height-to-width or length-to-diameter ratio) in a cross-section substantially parallel to or perpendicular to the vertical axis.

In certain embodiments, the ratio of $C_1$ to $A_2$ ($C_1 / A_2$) is greater than 1.2, or less than 0.8. In preferred embodiments, $C_1$ is configured to be in a range from about 1.2 to about 5.0 (representing elongated or anisotropic cells), while $A_2$ is configured to be in a range from about 0.8 to about 1.1 (representing substantially isotropic or spherical cells).

In another aspect, the variation between $C_1$ and $A_2$ at the boundary region creates a mechanical interlock or a controlled stress-transition zone between the first vertical layer and the second vertical layer. 

In some embodiments, the first cell aspect ratio $C_1$ represents cells oriented substantially parallel to the vertical axis, whereas the second cell aspect ratio $A_2$ represents cells oriented substantially perpendicular to the vertical axis or arranged in a randomized geometry. 

In additional embodiments, the foam-molded article may comprise a step-change in cell aspect ratio at the boundary region, or a localized micro-gradient transition zone within a predefined thickness (e.g., less than 2 mm) of the boundary region where $C_1$ transitions into $A_2$.

The first vertical layer and the second vertical layer may be formed from the same base polymer composition (e.g., polypropylene, polyethylene, polyurethane, or thermoplastic elastomers) or from different, mutually compatible polymer compositions. Furthermore, the first and second vertical layers may exhibit substantially identical bulk densities while possessing differing cell aspect ratios $C_1$ and $A_2$ at the boundary region, thereby uncoupling cell morphology from foam density.

### Advantageous Effects
The foam-molded article of the present disclosure offers several key advantages over conventional foam structures:
1. **Enhanced Delamination and Shear Resistance:** By controlling $C_1$ and $A_2$ at the boundary, stress concentrations at the interface are redistributed, significantly decreasing the likelihood of interfacial failure under shear, bending, or tensile loads.
2. **Tailored Energy Dissipation:** The distinct cell aspect ratios allow adjacent vertical layers to collapse, deform, or absorb energy at different force thresholds under compressive loading, providing a multi-stage or progressive energy-absorption profile.
3. **Optimized Strength-to-Weight Ratio:** Structural rigidity can be preferentially imparted in a specific direction (e.g., via elongated cells associated with $C_1$) without unnecessarily increasing the overall mass of the article or compromising the flexibility/cushioning provided by the layer associated with $A_2$.

***

### *Drafting Notes for the Patent Attorney/Agent:*
*   **Definitions:** Ensure that "vertical layer" and "cell aspect ratio" ($C_1$ and $A_2$) are explicitly defined in the *Detailed Description* (e.g., specifying whether measurement is taken via SEM, Micro-CT, or optical microscopy).
*   **Variable Consistency:** If $A_2$ stands for a specific parameter other than aspect ratio (e.g., Cell Area, Anisotropy index, or Aspect ratio of Layer 2), adjust the wording slightly to explicitly state: *"wherein $C_1$ represents the cell aspect ratio of the first layer and $A_2$ represents [the cell aspect ratio / structural parameter] of the second layer."*

---

# TECHNICAL SPECIFICATION: ANISOTROPIC MULTI-LAYER POLYURETHANE FOAM CUSHION ASSEMBLY

**Document ID:** SPEC-PU-MLC-004  
**Material Class:** Cellular Polyurethane (Flexible/Semi-Rigid Multi-Density Assembly)  
**Subject:** Cellular Morphology, Anisotropic Cell Orientation, and Microcellular Aspect Ratios  

---

## 1. System Overview & Coordinate Reference Frame

The cushion assembly consists of a three-layer laminated polyurethane structure designed to optimize load distribution, shear dampening, and posture support. 

To define cellular geometry, all orientations are referenced to a three-dimensional Cartesian coordinate system ($X, Y, Z$) based on two primary planar boundaries:
*   **Mounting Surface ($S_M$):** Defined as the horizontal base plane ($XY$-plane at $Z = 0$), interfacing with the structural pan.
*   **Back Surface ($S_B$):** Defined as the posterior vertical/inclined support plane ($XZ$-plane at $Y = 0$, inclined at angle $\phi = 95^\circ$ relative to $S_M$).

```
            +---------------------------------+
           /|                                /| 
          / |  Layer C (Surface / Comfort)  / |
         +--+------------------------------+--+
        /   |                             /   |  <-- Back Surface (S_B)
       /    |  Layer B (Intermediate)    /    |      [YZ/XZ-plane]
      +-----+---------------------------+     |
      |     |                           |     |
      |     |  Layer A (Base / Load)    |     |
      |     +---------------------------+-----+
      |    /                            |    /
      |   /                             |   / 
      |  /                              |  / 
      +---------------------------------+   <-- Mounting Surface (S_M) [XY-plane]
```

---

## 2. Microcellular Structural Specifications

Cell morphology is characterized by the **Cell Aspect Ratio ($R_c$)** and the **Primary Cell Vector ($\mathbf{V}_c$)**:
$$\text{Aspect Ratio } (R_c) = \frac{L_{\text{major}}}{L_{\text{minor}}}$$
*(Where $L_{\text{major}}$ is the length of the cell along its principal axis of elongation, and $L_{\text{minor}}$ is the maximum cell width orthogonal to the principal axis).*

---

### Layer A: High-Support Base Layer (Mounting Interface)
*Position: Adjacent to Mounting Surface ($S_M$), $0 \le Z \le 25\text{ mm}$*

*   **Polyurethane Type:** High-Resilience (HR) Cold-Cure Molded PU Foam.
*   **Target Density:** $60 \text{ kg/m}^3 \pm 3\%$.
*   **Cell Morphology:** Open-cell, highly anisotropic.
*   **Cell Aspect Ratio ($R_{cA}$):** **$2.2 : 1$ to $2.5 : 1$** (Highly elongated along the primary rise axis).
*   **Cell Orientation Angle ($\theta_A$):**
    *   **Relative to Mounting Surface ($S_M$):** Primary axis vector $\mathbf{V}_{cA}$ is oriented at **$90^\circ \pm 3^\circ$** (Normal to $S_M$).
    *   **Relative to Back Surface ($S_B$):** Primary axis vector $\mathbf{V}_{cA}$ is oriented at **$5^\circ \pm 3^\circ$** (Parallel to $S_B$).
*   **Functional Intent:** Maximum compressive modulus along the $Z$-axis to prevent bottoming-out while maintaining structural stability against lateral displacement parallel to $S_M$.

---

### Layer B: Transition Core Layer (Shear-Dampening Intermediate)
*Position: Intermediate Core, $25\text{ mm} < Z \le 60\text{ mm}$*

*   **Polyurethane Type:** MDI-based Flexible Viscoelastic/HR Hybrid PU Foam.
*   **Target Density:** $45 \text{ kg/m}^3 \pm 3\%$.
*   **Cell Morphology:** Semi-open cell, moderately anisotropic.
*   **Cell Aspect Ratio ($R_{cB}$):** **$1.5 : 1$ to $1.7 : 1$** (Moderately elongated).
*   **Cell Orientation Angle ($\theta_B$):**
    *   **Relative to Mounting Surface ($S_M$):** Primary axis vector $\mathbf{V}_{cB}$ is angled at **$45^\circ \pm 5^\circ$** sloping downward toward the rear ($S_B$).
    *   **Relative to Back Surface ($S_B$):** Primary axis vector $\mathbf{V}_{cB}$ is angled at **$50^\circ \pm 5^\circ$**.
*   **Functional Intent:** Off-axis cell alignment provides progressive load transfer between vertical pelvic forces and rearward lumbar forces, mitigating shear stress along the user's skin interface.

---

### Layer C: Surface Comfort Layer (Tactile Interface)
*Position: Top Surface, $60\text{ mm} < Z \le 85\text{ mm}$*

*   **Polyurethane Type:** Low-Unloading Viscoelastic (Memory) PU Foam.
*   **Target Density:** $50 \text{ kg/m}^3 \pm 2\%$.
*   **Cell Morphology:** Micro-porous, near-isotropic to slightly oblate.
*   **Cell Aspect Ratio ($R_{cC}$):** **$1.1 : 1$ to $1.2 : 1$** (Near-spherical).
*   **Cell Orientation Angle ($\theta_C$):**
    *   **Relative to Mounting Surface ($S_M$):** Primary axis vector $\mathbf{V}_{cC}$ is oriented at **$0^\circ \pm 10^\circ$** (Parallel to $S_M$).
    *   **Relative to Back Surface ($S_B$):** Primary axis vector $\mathbf{V}_{cC}$ is oriented at **$85^\circ \pm 10^\circ$** (Perpendicular to $S_B$).
*   **Functional Intent:** Uniform multi-directional pressure distribution ($X$-$Y$ displacement compliance) with minimum directional resistance upon initial contact.

---

## 3. Layer Property Matrix

| Parameter | Layer A (Base) | Layer B (Core) | Layer C (Top) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Thickness** | $25 \text{ mm}$ | $35 \text{ mm}$ | $20 \text{ mm}$ |
| **Cell Aspect Ratio ($R_c$)** | **$2.2:1 - 2.5:1$** | **$1.5:1 - 1.7:1$** | **$1.1:1 - 1.2:1$** |
| **Primary Vector Normal to $S_M$** | $90^\circ$ (Perpendicular) | $45^\circ$ (Oblique) | $0^\circ$ (Parallel) |
| **Primary Vector Normal to $S_B$** | $5^\circ$ (Parallel) | $50^\circ$ (Oblique) | $85^\circ$ (Perpendicular) |
| **Mean Cell Diameter ($L_{\text{major}}$)**| $450 \ \mu\text{m}$ | $320 \ \mu\text{m}$ | $180 \ \mu\text{m}$ |
| **Compression Load Deflection (40%)**| $4.5 \text{ kPa}$ | $2.8 \text{ kPa}$ | $1.1 \text{ kPa}$ |

---

## 4. Manufacturing & Orientation Control Requirements

1. **Free-Rise Directionality:**
   * **Layer A** must be harvested from the bun such that the free-rise vector of the reaction foaming process aligns directly with the normal of the cushion's mounting plane ($Z$-axis).
   * **Layer B** must be wire-cut via CNC at a $45^\circ$ angle relative to the original block free-rise axis to achieve the specified oblique cellular anisotropy.
